claims.text: The Origin of Species is Charles Darwin's argument that species were not each separately created but descended from earlier species, with natural selection as the main cause of change. It was published by John Murray in London in 1859 and is written as a long, non-technical book for educated readers rather than as a specialist paper.

claims.text: Darwin calls it an “Abstract”: a shortened version of a much larger work still unfinished. He says he was urged to publish it because his health was poor and because Alfred Russel Wallace, a naturalist working in the Malay archipelago, had reached almost the same conclusions.

citations.title: Introduction by Charles Darwin
citations.author: Charles Darwin
citations.quote: My work is now nearly finished; but as it will take me two or three more years to complete it, and as my health is far from strong, I have been urged to publish this Abstract.

citations.title: Introduction by Charles Darwin
citations.author: Charles Darwin
citations.quote: Mr. Wallace, who is now studying the natural history of the Malay archipelago, has arrived at almost exactly the same general conclusions that I have on the origin of species.

claims.text: Darwin opens with an epigraph from William Whewell, a Cambridge philosopher of science, saying that natural events come from the establishment of general laws, not from separate acts of divine intervention. This was how many educated Britons already thought of the natural world, and Darwin wished to place his theory inside that outlook.

citations.title: Epigraph from Whewell
citations.author: Charles Darwin
citations.quote: we can perceive that events are brought about not by insulated interpositions of Divine power, exerted in each particular case, but by the establishment of general laws.

claims.text: Darwin's method came from the geologist Charles Lyell and the philosopher Sir John Herschel: explain the past only by causes that can be observed working now. Darwin held that any theory of species had to meet this standard.

claims.text: Darwin was recommended as a gentleman companion and naturalist for Captain Robert FitzRoy's round-the-world voyage of HMS Beagle. What he saw in South America, in the distribution of living animals and in their relation to fossil ones, set him thinking about the origin of species.

claims.text: Darwin began patiently collecting facts on the question in 1837 and wrote a sketch of his conclusions in 1844. He read Malthus's Essay on Population in October 1838 and saw at once that favourable variations would be preserved and unfavourable ones destroyed.

claims.text: In 1858 Wallace sent Darwin from Ternate (in the East Indies) an essay containing the same theory. Darwin's friends Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged for it to be read at the Linnean Society of London, together with extracts from Darwin's own earlier manuscripts, on 1 July 1858.

claims.text: Darwin's friends Hooker, Thomas Henry Huxley and the American botanist Asa Gray sent him their first impressions of the book. Even sympathetic scientists balked: Lyell would not openly endorse the theory and Herschel rejected key elements of it.

claims.text: Malthus argued that human population grows geometrically while resources grow arithmetically. Darwin carried the idea of a struggle for existence from human society into plant and animal life.

citations.title: Population Theory: Malthus's Influence on the Scope of Evolution (Science and Its Times)
citations.quote: Malthusian principle states that populations grow geometrically while resources grow only arithmetically.

citations.title: Darwinism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: This tendency is checked, to use the language of Thomas Malthus’ On the Principle of Population, by limited resources, disease, predation, and so on, creating a struggle for existence among the members of a species.

claims.text: Darwin's Edinburgh mentor Robert Grant taught evolutionary ideas derived from the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and from Darwin's own grandfather Erasmus Darwin, so the possibility of evolution was familiar to Darwin before the Origin.

citations.title: Darwinism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: Grant expounded evolutionary ideas derived from Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and Charles’ grandfather.
